learningObjective: Analyze a shared-memory transpose kernel and identify which access pattern causes a 32-way bank conflict; know the padding-based mitigation.

canonicalClaims.claim: In a `__shared__ float tile[32][32]` arrangement on sm_80 (32 banks × 4-byte width), a warp accessing a column of the tile (fixed inner index, varying outer index across threads) causes a 32-way bank conflict; padding the inner dimension to 33 shifts the column stride off the bank period and eliminates the conflict.
conditions: The compiler does not reorder accesses to change the mapping.
nonImplications: Does not imply that padding is always the right fix; SMEM-swizzle patterns can achieve the same without wasted SMEM.
Does not imply that the row-store side of a naive transpose conflicts (it does not).

misconceptions.claim: Both the row write and the transposed read are conflict-free because CUDA hardware supports multicast for arbitrary addresses.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Shared memory supports broadcast (all threads read the same address) but not multicast (distinct addresses within the same bank). Distinct-address bank conflicts serialize.

misconceptions.claim: The write causes the bank conflict; the read is fine because it uses the transposed pattern.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Row writes are stride-1 across banks and conflict-free; column reads hit the same bank across all warp lanes.

misconceptions.claim: nvcc automatically inserts SMEM padding when it detects bank conflicts.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The compiler cannot change user-declared SMEM layout; the fix must be source-level.

misconceptions.claim: Bank conflicts are a global-memory phenomenon.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Bank conflicts are strictly a shared-memory phenomenon; global memory has coalescing rules instead.

implementationFacts: `tile[r][c]` maps to bank `c mod 32` for float type
Padding `tile[32][33]` breaks 32-way conflict on column reads
performanceScenarios: Transpose, GEMM SMEM tiling, and reduction tree kernels all rely on conflict-free SMEM access patterns; padding, swizzling, or asymmetric shapes are the standard mitigations.
